Article Title: A federal judge rules Brooke Rollins' religious emails to roughly 100,000 USDA employees unconstitutional and restricts the use of her official account
Article Text:
US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.

Judge says Rollins crossed boundaries with Christian messages

USDA considers appeal as religious messaging sparks debate

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A US federal judge has ordered Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to stop sending religious messages to employees through her official government email account, ruling that her communications crossed boundaries by assuming that staff members shared her Christian beliefs.US District Judge Trina Thompson issued the order on Thursday while granting a preliminary injunction sought by federal employees who accused Rollins of using her position to promote Christianity within the Department of Agriculture (USDA). The judge said the secretary must recognise limits when communicating religious messages and cannot use her official authority to pressure subordinates."The Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognise certain boundaries when communicating religious messages," Thompson wrote in her ruling.The case was brought by seven USDA employees from different religious backgrounds, including those who do not identify with any religion. They alleged that Rollins had sent increasingly religious messages to the department's entire workforce, making employees feel excluded and pressured to conform to her beliefs.According to the complaint, Rollins began sending department-wide holiday emails shortly after taking office.Some of the messages included references to Jesus Christ, Christmas and the resurrection of Jesus.In a Christmas message sent on December 23, 2025, Rollins said that the spirit of generosity came from "the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ".In another message sent on Easter, April 5, 2026, she described the occasion as "the greatest story ever told" and referred to employees as being like the first disciples who encountered the risen Christ.The employees argued that the messages amounted to government-sponsored religious promotion and violated the First Amendment's protections against the establishment of religion.Thompson agreed that the communications went too far, finding that they created pressure on employees to accept or appear to share the secretary's religious beliefs.The judge also took issue with Rollins' repeated use of words such as "we", "us" and "our" in the messages, saying the language suggested that employees universally shared her Christian beliefs. She noted that the emails did not acknowledge employees who followed other religions or held no religious beliefs.The court also rejected the argument that employees could simply ignore the messages, pointing out that Rollins used the same official email account to communicate important departmental information, including agency restructuring and government shutdown plans."Why should the secretary be exempt from her own rules? The buck stops with Secretary Rollins," Thompson wrote, adding that her senior position warranted greater scrutiny because she sat at the top of the agency's hierarchy.The judge clarified that the order did not prevent Rollins from expressing her faith in her personal capacity or discussing religion with colleagues who were interested.The USDA said it was evaluating all available options, including filing an appeal, and described the ruling as a "completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary".The department had argued that Rollins was merely sharing her personal views about religious holidays and was neither conducting religious exercises nor forcing employees to follow her beliefs.However, Thompson pointed to the department's own November 2025 guidance on religious expression in the workplace, saying Rollins should follow the boundaries outlined in her own directives. The guidance allows employees to discuss their faith with interested colleagues but prohibits persistent unwanted religious advances and the use of official authority to pressure subordinates.The ruling comes amid a wider debate over the role of religion in the Trump administration. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has incorporated Christian prayer into activities at the Pentagon, while critics have accused administration officials of blurring the separation between religion and government.Advocates of church-state separation have also raised concerns over religious messaging by senior officials and the use of government platforms to promote Christianity.The USDA ruling, however, does not prevent Rollins from practising or expressing her faith privately. It restricts the use of her official government communication channels in ways that could amount to religious coercion in the workplace.
Article Summary: Judge says Rollins cannot use her position to pressure employees into following her religious beliefs. The ruling is in response to complaints that the messages violated the First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The judge says the ruling does not prevent Rollins from expressing her faith in private.

Article Title: UK acts to secure thousands of commercial fridges after Europe cyberattacks
Article Text:
File photo: An employee works on empty freezers in a store where a cyberattack has taken down several of its freezers (Representative Image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Britain has carried out a major cybersecurity operation to protect tens of thousands of commercial fridges and freezers from potential hacking. Recent attacks on refrigeration systems across Europe spoiled food worth millions of euros and disrupted supermarkets.The operation involved major supermarket chains, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, with thousands of devices used to control refrigeration systems taken offline as a precaution. In some cases, staff were asked to physically disconnect internet cables and monitor temperatures manually, the BBC reported.The vulnerability was discovered in late October by ethical hackers at British firm Omega Systems, who examined the security of refrigeration controllers made by Resource Data Management (RDM). Experts at Pen Test Partners helped verify the weakness and alert authorities.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency joined the effort to warn businesses and plug the security gaps. IT teams at major supermarket chains were diverted to the task, with one employee telling the BBC that hundreds of devices were taken offline each day over a week.The urgency followed a series of attacks on commercial refrigeration systems in Europe. In France, hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites were hit in October after hackers targeted temperature-control systems made by Danish firm Danfoss. A further wave in early November affected stores across seven European countries, with Belgium and Luxembourg among the worst hit.French intelligence and cybersecurity agencies blamed Iran's Revolutionary Guards for the October attack, which reportedly affected around 700 commercial sites and triggered 15 fires after hackers raised temperatures in refrigeration systems. Tehran has denied the accusation.Security researchers warned that Britain's refrigeration controllers had weaknesses, including problems involving weak passwords. However, RDM disputed comparisons with the European attacks, saying exploiting its systems would have required physical access to specific hardware.RDM chief executive Ged Evans said the vulnerability was identified in a test environment and that the assessment involved dismantling the company's hardware. He said the company had already released initial software patches, contacted customers and recommended steps to reduce risks. RDM also said it had found no evidence of malicious activity on its controllers.The BBC said the operation had been kept under wraps to avoid alerting potential attackers before businesses could secure their systems.
Article Summary: Operation involved major supermarket chains, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums. Staff were asked to physically disconnect internet cables and monitor temperatures manually. Vulnerability discovered in late October by ethical hackers at British firm Omega Systems. Security researchers warned that Britain's refrigeration controllers had weaknesses.

Article Title: Archaeologists on a remote Japanese island uncovered the foundations of a mysterious 900-year-old octagonal building, possibly a Buddhist pagoda, beside evidence of roof tiles shipped about 1,000 kilo
Article Text:
Aerial view of the Ōsato archaeological site on Kuroshima Island, Japan, highlighting the newly discovered outline of a 900-year-old octagonal foundation. Area under solid white lines indicate excavated section, while reconstructed portions are highlighted by dotted lines. Credit: Kagoshima International University / Professor Satoshi Nakazono

Connections to China

Could the structure be religious in origin?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Beyond religion, trade routes revealed

The abyss underwater is vast and mystical, it consists of creatures that stay unknown but glow the brightest, microorrganisms that sustain the ecosystem or metals and elements that are crucial for the world above. The world underwater is a mystery that keeps unfolding with constant efforts of the scientific community. Professor Satoshi Nakazono of Kagoshima International University has been trying to expose one such secret site on a Japanese Island since 2014. He has uncovered ceramics, roof tiles and other objects originating from China and different regions of Japan.There has been discovery of the foundations of an unusual octagonal structure which is suspected to be the remains of a Buddhist pagoda or religious building constructed around 900 years ago. The site is known as the Ōsato archaeological site located on Kuroshima, which is one of the islands of Mishima Village in Kagoshima Prefecture.Within an area of levelled ground which was previously recorded at the archeological site, a new octagonal arrangement has been identified. The absence of the upperstructure, however, has left the archeologists wondering the purpose of this unique building. The structure is approximately 8.9 metres between opposite corners of its upper section.While individual sides measure around 3.4 metres each. The structure also contains a lower section that is wider, measuring between 10 and 11 metres.There have been previous discoveries of imported roof tiles from Ōsato, the recent findings can help in explaining the questions behind them. While the tiles are characteristic of China’s Southern Song period, Kuroshima is the southernmost known location in Japan where this kind of tiles have been found. Other regions which were closely associated with medieval maritime trade between Japan and China, like Hakata and Kyushu have revealed similar tiles.Earlier research, in 2015, made the discovery of tiles made from the same moulds at Ningbo in China. After further research involving chemical analysis of the samples from the two sites, it was revealed that the examples discovered in Japan had also been produced there. This is especially insightful as it implies that the building materials travelled approximately 1,000 kilometres by sea before reaching Japan.The latest research has raised the possibility that these imported tiles might have been used to roof an octagonal religious structure at Ōsato. Further research, if it confirms the usage, will point to not just transport of construction material but the propagation of architectural styles between the two countries.There have been estimations of the structure being religious, specifically of Buddhist origin. This is because octagonal architecture has associations with Buddhist religious buildings in Japan and China, like pagodas and religious halls. After studying the plan and archeological context, Nakazono and his team have made inferences that suggest Ōsato structure may have housed a pagoda or another sacred building. The structure is also placed within an area believed to have held religious significance and the discovery of Chinese-style roof tiles.The structure revealed has been compared with other similar octagonal religious architecture elsewhere in East Asia. Two of them are present in Japan itself- the nine-storey pagoda formerly standing at Hōshō-ji Temple in Kyoto and the three-storey pagoda at Anraku-ji Temple in Nagano.While the comparisons help in finding the origins of the discovery, the true nature remains uncertain.Kuroshima's location along the maritime routes of southwestern Japan may explain how imported goods found their way to these otherwise small and remote islands of Japan. The ceramics unearthed at Ōsato suggest that its residents were connected to wider trading networks, rather than being isolated from the outside world. Nearby Iōjima also played a role in regional commerce during the medieval period, when it was known for its sulphur trade, an important commodity exported to China.
Article Summary: Archaeologists have discovered the foundations of an octagonal structure on Kuroshima Island, Japan. It is suspected to be the remains of a Buddhist pagoda or religious building constructed around 900 years ago. Professor Satoshi Nakazono of Kagoshima International University has been trying to expose one such secret site on a Japanese Island since 2014.

Article Title: A Facebook request brought a boy with leukaemia 2,000 patches from across the US; his family later created a project that sends free patch-covered jackets and tote bags to children with cancer
Article Text:
PC: Oliver Patch Project

How Oliver received 2,000 patches during cancer treatment

The patches helped Oliver feel supported during treatment

‘Oliver Patch Project’ has reached children across all 50 states

Gorilla, bald eagle and polar bear patches marked different treatment stages

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When Oliver Burkhardt was diagnosed with leukaemia, his father, Brian, wanted to find a way to bring some happiness into his life during chemotherapy. He turned to Facebook, asking friends to send decorative patches that Oliver could collect and sew onto a jacket.What began as a small request soon reached people beyond the family’s circle. Within a month, Oliver had received 2,000 patches, about 70% of them from strangers. The gesture gave Oliver something to look forward to during treatment. According to The Associated Press, the experience inspired the family to establish the ‘Oliver Patch Project’, which sends free patch-decorated jackets or tote bags to children with cancer across the United States.Oliver’s father first thought of the idea in 2020, shortly after his son was diagnosed. Brian noticed some patches lying in a desk drawer and thought receiving similar ones in the mail might cheer Oliver up.Friends could send them even during COVID-19 lockdowns,Brian said, “It’s an easy ask. They can drop a patch in an envelope and, in return, it gave Oliver something to look forward to. Checking the mail every day would get him off the sofa.”Brian shared his request on Facebook, and friends began passing it on to others. The first patch to arrive was a kangaroo. Soon, more patches followed, turning a small request into a much bigger response. Around 2,000 patches arrived that month, with 70% coming from strangers.Oliver surprisingly said, “I was like, ‘Wow, this is all for me?’ I was like genuinely super surprised. They were all different colors and they all had nice notes, like ‘Hope you feel better.’”As he continued treatment, his parents began sewing the patches onto jackets while sitting with him in his hospital room.Oliver wore his denim jacket to hospital, with around 50 patches chosen from the thousands that had arrived. They included designs linked to Pokémon, Superman, NASA, police, fire and military services, as well as classic rock bands.The jacket became a source of comfort during treatment and helped start conversations with nurses. His parents also decorated their own jackets, showing that they were a team.Oliver said, “I knew people were looking out for me, they gave me positive vibes, that people loved me.”Seeing the effect on their son, Oliver and his parents decided that other children going through cancer treatment might also appreciate a jacket of their own.The family launched the ‘Oliver Patch Project’ after reaching out to designer friends, who sent 300 possible patch designs within a day.As of 2024, three years after its launch, the charity had provided more than 1,600 children, from infancy to 19 years old, with a free denim jacket or tote bag. Each child or their parents selected 20 patches from the programme’s website.The charity then sent another patch by mail every month. As of 2024, children with cancer from all 50 states had joined the nationwide programme, and about 30 children enrolled each week. The project was limited to the United States, although funding had also been secured to send patches to sick children taking part in experimental drug trials in the US and 18 other countries.The project also sent families a box of 13 milestone patches to give children during common cancer treatments or when they experienced side effects.Designs included a gorilla for starting chemotherapy, a bald eagle for hair loss and a polar bear for fever. A child could work towards receiving an ‘I Rang the Bell’ patch after completing a round of treatment.Siblings received special patches too, after Oliver’s parents recognised that his younger brother, Peter, also needed attention during the family’s difficult period. The charity was supported by donors and foundations, while clothing company Perry Ellis donated jackets and tote bags.
Article Summary: Oliver Burkhardt was diagnosed with leukaemia in 2020. His father, Brian, wanted to bring some happiness into his life during chemotherapy. He turned to Facebook, asking friends to send decorative patches that Oliver could collect and sew onto a jacket. Within a month, Oliver had received 2,000 patches, about 70% of them from strangers. The experience inspired the family to establish the ‘Oliver Patch Project’

Article Title: A Scottish couple argued that a row of 17 trees and shrubs on their property was not legally a hedge, but officials rejected their appeal and ordered them to reduce its height after neighbours complai
Article Text:
How the dispute began

Why officials rejected the appeal

The couple’s argument for preserving the trees

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens to the hedge now?

A property dispute in East Lothian, Scotland, has ended with a couple being ordered to reduce the height of a row of trees and shrubs after authorities ruled that the planting qualified as a high hedge under Scottish law. Professor Angus Macdonald and Dr Patricia Macdonald had challenged the order, arguing that their garden boundary consisted of 17 individual trees and shrubs rather than a hedge. However, a Scottish Government reporter upheld the council’s decision following an inspection of the properties. The case was reported by STV News and Midlothian View, with further details of Scotland’s high hedge legislation available through the Scottish Government.The disagreement arose at the couple’s property in Ashgrove, Musselburgh, which falls within the Musselburgh Conservation Area. Their neighbours approached East Lothian Council, complaining that the boundary vegetation was growing over their property, dropping leaves, berries and other debris, and significantly restricting their access to natural light.Following the complaint, East Lothian Council issued a High Hedge Notice requiring the couple to reduce the height of the planting.The Macdonalds challenged the decision before Scottish Ministers. Their appeal centred on the classification of the vegetation, maintaining that the boundary was made up of a varied collection of closely planted trees and shrubs rather than a conventional hedge.The Scottish Government reporter visited the gardens before reaching a decision. Under Scotland’s High Hedges (Scotland) Act 2013, a high hedge can consist of a row of two or more trees or shrubs that exceeds two metres in height and forms a barrier to light.The legislation does not require the vegetation to consist of a single species or resemble a traditionally trimmed garden hedge. What matters is whether the planting meets the legal criteria and affects the reasonable enjoyment of neighbouring property.After examining the boundary, the reporter concluded that the trees and shrubs met the definition. The planting was found to restrict light and interfere with the neighbouring property’s reasonable enjoyment, supporting the council’s decision to issue the notice.The Macdonalds also argued that removing or substantially reducing the vegetation would affect the character and environmental value of their garden. They maintained that the trees and ivy made an important contribution to the appearance of Ashgrove, particularly because the property lies within a conservation area. Their appeal highlighted the practical benefits of the planting, including protection from extreme weather, improved air quality and shade during periods of high temperatures.They also pointed to the wildlife supported by the garden, citing more than 50 species of birds, over 10 species of butterflies and numerous bees and other pollinating insects. However, the reporter concluded that the planting could continue to provide environmental and visual benefits even after its height had been reduced.Under the council’s notice, the boundary planting must be cut back and maintained at a maximum height of 2.5 metres, approximately eight feet. The order does not cover every tree along the boundary. An ash tree and a willow tree, positioned at opposite ends of the boundary wall, have been excluded from the required trimming.The couple have also been given additional time to complete the work. The revised compliance period is intended to ensure that the trimming takes place outside the bird-nesting season. The decision brings the appeal to a close, although it highlights how Scottish legislation can apply to mixed rows of trees and shrubs, even when property owners do not consider the planting to be a hedge.
Article Summary: Professor Angus Macdonald and Dr Patricia Macdonald had challenged the order. They argued that their garden boundary consisted of 17 individual trees and shrubs rather than a hedge. A Scottish Government reporter upheld the council’s decision following an inspection of the properties.

Article Title: An Egyptian writer who spent more than six years imprisoned won America's National Book Award for nonfiction, but could not attend the New York ceremony after US officials denied him a visitor visa
Article Text:
Image courtesy: Instagram/@abdelrahman_elgendy95

A memoir shaped by revolution and imprisonment

ElGendy's editor at Hogarth, Helen Thomaides, accepted the award on his behalf.

Visa denial became part of the award-night story

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An Egyptian writer who spent more than six years in prison for his political activism has won one of America's biggest literary honours. But Abdelrahman ElGendy could not attend the award ceremony in New York because US officials denied him a visitor visa. ElGendy won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction for his memoir, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. The award was announced on November 18 at the 77th National Book Awards ceremony at Cipriani Wall Street in New York.According to Los Angeles Times, ElGendy was absent because the US consular office denied his visitor visa application. He is now living in the United Kingdom after leaving the US in April 2025, fearing that he could be deported to Egypt, where he had previously spent more than six years as a political prisoner.His editor at Hogarth, Helen Thomaides, accepted the award on his behalf and read a statement from the writer. “If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you,” ElGendy wrote.He recalled imagining, while in his prison cell in Egypt, that he would one day write a memoir about his experiences. He later began hoping that the book might win an award. The recognition came, but he could not be present to receive it.Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming recounts ElGendy's experiences as a political prisoner in Egypt following the country's 2011 revolution. The book explores his imprisonment, personal relationships, family and efforts to rebuild his life.The National Book Foundation's judges described the memoir as a story of survival and resistance. Their citation called it a “lyric testament to survival and resistance” and highlighted the book's account of a father-son relationship built around love, endurance and hope. The book's title draws inspiration from the Arab protest song ‘Sawfa Nabqua Huna,’ which translates as “We Will Remain Here”.In his acceptance statement, ElGendy dedicated the award to people affected by political imprisonment and displacement. He specifically mentioned Palestinians, political prisoners in Egypt and people who have disappeared into US immigration detention.He wrote that he wanted to redirect attention to “the more than 60,000 political prisoners still behind the bars of Egypt’s military dictatorship bankrolled by the U.S. government”. He also referred to “the tens of thousands of souls disappeared in ICE concentration camps”. These were ElGendy's words in his acceptance statement, read at the ceremony by Thomaides.The visa issue had already attracted attention before the ceremony. In an essay for The New Yorker, ElGendy had explained that he could not obtain permission to travel to the US for the event.His absence also became part of the discussion around the 2026 awards. According to Publishers Weekly, Thomaides said the author was “not able to return even as a celebrated visitor and it’s ultimately our loss as a nation”.There was also a separate debate about whether ElGendy met the National Book Award's US residency requirement. As per a New York Times report, his eligibility was questioned because he had left the country. The National Book Foundation defended its decision, explaining that his publisher had confirmed he was a legal and tax-paying US resident who temporarily left in 2025 because he feared for his safety amid immigration arrests.The foundation said it had determined that the information provided met its eligibility rules. The awards had expanded eligibility to non-US citizens in 2024, according to Publishers Weekly.
Article Summary: Abdelrahman ElGendy won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction for his memoir, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. The award was announced on November 18 at the 77th National Book Awards ceremony at Cipriani Wall Street in New York. He was absent because the US consular office denied his visitor visa application. He is now living in the United Kingdom after leaving the US in April 2025.

Article Title: A Windsor, Connecticut player bought a 200X scratch-off ticket at Bloom’s Discount Liquor and won $1 million, but under a new state rule, the winner’s name will stay secret unless they agree to go pub
Article Text:
Why the winner’s identity will remain private

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A routine stop at a liquor store in Windsor, Connecticut, turned into a life-changing moment for one lottery player who walked away with a $1 million scratch-off prize. The winning ticket was purchased at Bloom’s Discount Liquor, but the identity of the lucky player may never become public unless they choose to reveal it. According to the Connecticut Lottery and reporting by the Hartford Courant, the Windsor resident claimed the top prize in the 200X 4th Edition scratch-off game on Monday, November 16. The player had purchased the $20 ticket from the store at 576 Windsor Avenue and opted to receive a one-time cash payment rather than spread the winnings over several years. The $750,000 payment is the game’s gross cash value, before taxes. The winner could instead have received the full $1 million through an annuity paid over 20 years. The odds of winning the top prize were listed as one in 800,000, making it a particularly rare win.The decision not to identify the winner follows a change in Connecticut’s lottery disclosure rules that took effect on October 1, 2025. Under Public Act 25-112, the Connecticut Lottery Corporation must obtain a winner’s prior written consent before publishing their name or address.The requirement also covers the publication of winners’ photographs.Previously, the lottery could publish winners’ names, although individuals could request to have their names removed from its online winners list. The revised law makes consent the starting point instead. The law does not, however, prevent disclosure under Connecticut’s Freedom of Information Act. It specifically preserves that provision, meaning the restriction applies to the lottery’s own publication of winners’ details rather than creating an absolute guarantee of anonymity in every circumstance.The Connecticut Lottery’s official winners list confirms the November 16 claim, identifying Windsor as the winner’s hometown, Bloom’s Discount Liquor as the retailer and 200X 4TH EDITION as the game. The winner’s name has not been published. The game offered three $1 million top prizes. According to the lottery’s prize information updated on November 16, all three had been claimed, with the game reaching its scheduled end date that day.
Article Summary: Winning ticket was purchased at Bloom’s Discount Liquor in Windsor, Connecticut. The odds of winning the top prize were listed as one in 800,000, making it a particularly rare win. The winner opted to receive a one-time cash payment rather than spread the winnings over several years.

A massive fire ripped through a commercial building on Thailand's southern resort island of Phuket early on Monday, killing at least 11 people and leaving 16 others injured, police told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the early hours of the morning and quickly spread to several nearby buildings, triggering a major firefighting operation.The fire erupted at around 3.17am local time (2017 GMT) at a shophouse housing a vehicle rental business. Firefighters battled the flames for nearly two hours before bringing the blaze under control, Thai authorities said.Of the 16 injured, 15 were Thai nationals while one was from Myanmar, police said. No tourists were among those killed or injured in the incident.The building is located in a town area near Patong, one of Phuket's most popular beach destinations on the island's western coast. The incident raised concerns as the fire spread beyond the building where it first broke out, engulfing several neighbouring structures.The cause of the fire remains under investigation, with authorities yet to establish what triggered the blaze.The incident comes just four months after a deadly fire at a bar in Bangkok claimed at least 27 lives, highlighting another major fire tragedy in Thailand.Make the intro more directRemove repeated fire detailsUse a sharper news structure

Article Title: GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play
Article Text:
GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play

Lander Allgood and Connor Folkers plan extended breaks for GTA 6 release

GTA flu: Why some gamers are planning to call in sick

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, November 19. Some have already booked their paid leave, while others are considering calling in sick to spend the day playing the long-awaited game. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the ‘GTA flu’ online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.For some players, the GTA 6 launch is worth planning their entire week around. Lander Allgood, a 26-year-old environmental specialist from the Dallas-Fort Worth area, requested two weeks of paid time off in July so he could enjoy the release.Allgood, who has played GTA 5 since he was around 13, compared the new game’s arrival to a major scientific achievement.“We’re basically witnessing, I mean, the Apollo space program of video games,” Allgood told USA TODAY.However, gaming is not his only responsibility. He plans to spend time with his two-year-old son and has arranged for his parents to look after the child from Thursday through Sunday. Once his son goes to bed, Allgood expects to spend hours playing.He is hoping to put in at least 20 hours over the weekend.Connor Folkers, a 22-year-old IT administrator from Iowa, has also arranged his schedule around the launch. He requested leave from November 19 through Thanksgiving and expects to spend more than 24 hours playing.For Folkers, getting enough time with the game before seeing other people’s reactions is important. He wants to experience the story and gameplay without online discussions shaping his opinion.“Really how I treat this game is sort of like a cultural event. You’re going to see this, I presume, everywhere online, whether it be story components or gameplay components, so I want to make sure I have enough time to really experience it for myself without the outside influencing my opinions on it,” Folkers told USA TODAY.He also compared the release to the Super Bowl, explaining how important the event has become for gaming enthusiasts.Not everyone is being upfront about taking a day off. Some players are planning to report sick on November 19 instead of requesting paid leave in advance.GameSquare surveyed 1,000 full-time US employees who identified as gamers. Its findings showed that 10% planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Among those considering leave, 36% said they would call in sick.BambooHR also found that nearly one in five salaried US workers planned to take time off for the release. Its figures showed that 32% of Gen Z employees and 27% of millennials intended to use paid leave to play.Nicole Csiszar, BambooHR’s director of HR, told USA TODAY that taking planned leave is a normal way for employees to enjoy their time away from work.“That’s a healthy sign,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “It means people are using PTO the way it’s meant to be used, to step away and do something they enjoy.”She also pointed out why some might choose to call in sick instead.“Requesting PTO in advance means submitting it, waiting on approval and sometimes explaining why you want the day,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “Calling in sick is one message that morning.”However, not every gamer is willing to put work aside. Ryan Van Dusen, a 42-year-old fifth-grade teacher from Michigan, has no plans to miss classes for the game. He is instead looking forward to playing during the Thanksgiving holiday.“My kids are expected to be in the classroom. I can’t take a day off from my students for this. This is preposterous,” Van Dusen told USA TODAY with a laugh. “In theory, Grand Theft Auto should be a small thing compared to work, family, things that are bigger. I think it’s healthy and good for us to have these small things that we can be excited for too and just to look forward to.”
Article Summary: Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the 'GTA flu' online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.

Fire outside Met stadium

A fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season.Videos shared on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising near the stadium in East Rutherford and drifting over the playing field. One video also captured flames and black smoke erupting from the area near the venue.New Jersey State Police said troopers responded to a report of smoke shortly after 5:50 pm near Lot A and the stadium's American Express gate. They found a fire in an empty postgame tent, according to a report by Fox 5 New York.Fire crews brought the second-alarm blaze under control. No injuries or further damage were reported, while the cause of the fire was not immediately known.ESPN reporter Rich Cimini posted on social media that an announcement had been made inside the stadium about a “structure fire” near the adjacent train station. He later advised people to stay away from the stadium's east plaza, on the train station side, as smoke spread across the venue.Around 20 minutes later, he posted that the “situation has been resolved”.An NJ Transit spokesperson, quoted by NY Post said the fire did not disrupt train services in the area.The blaze broke out hours after the Jets lost 31-12 to the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium. The defeat marked their fifth straight loss, leaving them with a 2-8 record for the season.The Jets struggled against the Bills, who secured a 19-point victory. The loss extended New York's losing streak and added to a difficult season for the team.
Article Summary: Fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday. The blaze sent thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season. No injuries or further damage were reported. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Article Title: 'He is my friend': Trump, Putin hold talks ahead of trilateral meeting with Xi on APEC sidelines

Ukraine is losing. Ukraine and Russia are losing 25,000 souls per month, so we'll be talking about that. challenging international environment."Russian-Chinese political cooperation is working favourably and constructively in a difficult political situation," Putin stated."We are committed to constructive approaches to form a fairer multipolar world order," he added.The two leaders also discussed the need to expand cooperation across sectors, with Xi describing their partnership as a model of equality, mutual respect and mutually beneficial cooperation.According to Russian media reports, the discussions continued over a working breakfast in Shenzhen on Wednesday.Putin also addressed business representatives at the APEC CEO Summit, where he criticised the use of tariffs, sanctions and export restrictions as instruments of geopolitical and economic pressure.He argued that countries were increasingly seeking greater economic sovereignty and independence amid changes in the global geopolitical landscape."The regional model serves as a vivid example of strengthening a fairer, more democratic and equal world order," Putin said, referring to developments in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president criticised attempts by established economic powers to restrict the growth of important diplomatic platform for Washington, Moscow and Beijing to engage on issues ranging from nuclear security to regional conflicts and the future of the global economic order.

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: A Vermont landowner bought land to protect her privacy, but neighbours who used it for decades as a driveway, garden, and recreation space won ownership in a Supreme Court ruling
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How did a privacy buffer become the centre of a property dispute

What did a 2023 survey reveal about the disputed property

Driveway, garden and outdoor activities strengthen neighbours' ownership claim

Supreme Court upholds neighbours' ownership through constructive possession

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Disclaimer:

This article is based on the Vermont Supreme Court's ruling in Deborah Tarrant v. Christopher Bartels and Amelia Bartels. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the property dispute or the claims made by either party.

A Vermont homeowner bought vacant lots between her lakeside property and her neighbours’ land in 1988, intending to create a privacy buffer. However, the neighbours and their predecessor had already been using parts of the disputed area for years. Their activities included extending a driveway and turnaround, parking vehicles, maintaining a garden and rock steps, and using the land for outdoor recreation.The homeowner later challenged their claim to the strip, which measured about one-tenth of an acre. According to the Vermont Supreme Court's February Term, 2026 ruling in Deborah Tarrant v. Christopher Bartels and Amelia Bartels, the court upheld the ruling granting the neighbours ownership of the disputed land. In 2023, a survey confirmed that the disputed strip was part of her property.The homeowner acquired her lakeshore property in 1968. Her neighbours’ predecessor, Mr Gennari, bought the property to the south in 1979. In 1988, she purchased the vacant lots between the two properties to create a privacy buffer. The land lay between a road to the east and Lake Champlain to the west.Mr Gennari later sold his property to his daughter and son-in-law in 2019.The disputed strip measured about one-tenth of an acre and was marked by iron pipes along its northern side.Mr Gennari found the pipes when he bought his property and believed they marked its northern boundary.The neighbours’ driveway and turnaround extended into the disputed strip. They also parked cars and a recreational vehicle there, held parties and played outdoor games. Their other activities included reseeding the lawn several times, maintaining rock stairs and a garden, and using part of the area for a greywater field. The neighbours and their predecessor had used the land continuously from at least the early 1980s.The homeowner did not know until 2003 that the driveway extended onto land for which she held the legal title. In 2023, the plaintiff commissioned a survey that identified the strip as part of her property. The survey prompted the ownership dispute.The case began in the Chittenden Unit's civil division. The homeowner filed a lawsuit in September 2023, seeking a declaration that she owned the disputed land and damages for the removal of trees. The neighbours argued that their predecessor had acquired ownership through adverse possession.Under Vermont law, “To achieve title through adverse possession, a claimant must demonstrate that possession of the land was open, notorious, hostile and continuous throughout the statutory period of fifteen years.”The court considered the driveway, turnaround, tree cutting, greywater field, rock stairs, and garden as evidence that the land was used openly, as an owner would. The court also found that permission granted in 2003 did not affect the claim because the 15-year period had already passed.The homeowner appealed, arguing that the neighbours’ use was not sufficiently visible or extensive and that factual disputes remained. The Supreme Court rejected those arguments, explaining that the test was whether the activities would put a reasonably prudent person on notice, not whether the homeowner could see them from her house or the road.The Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favour of the neighbours, Christopher and Amelia Bartels. It upheld the finding that they had acquired ownership through constructive possession. Under this doctrine, a claimant can gain possession of an entire plot by occupying part of it in qualifying circumstances. The trial court relied on both clear boundaries and colour of title. The Supreme Court affirmed the colour of title, saying that the ground applied even if the clarity of the boundary markers was disputed.It also found that the neighbours' predecessor, Mr Gennari, had acted under colour of title, meaning he believed the iron pipes marked the boundary of his property. The Supreme Court therefore upheld the ruling granting the neighbours ownership of the entire disputed strip.
Article Summary: A Vermont homeowner bought vacant lots between her lakeside property and her neighbours’ land in 1988, intending to create a privacy buffer. However, the neighbours and their predecessor had already been using parts of the disputed area for years. Their activities included extending a driveway and turnaround, parking vehicles, maintaining a garden and rock steps, and using the land for outdoor recreation. The homeowner later challenged their claim to the strip, which measured about one-tenth of an acre. The Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favour of the neighbours, Christopher and Amelia Bartels.

Article Title: Trump appears nearly 200 times in Biden’s memoir, book revisits bitter 2024 presidential race
Article Text:
Joe Biden meets US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House (File photo)

Biden stands by 2024 re-election bid

Trump looms over Biden’s account of presidency

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US president Donald Trump may have succeeded Joe Biden in the White House, but he has also loomed large over the former US president’s account of his time in office. Biden mentions Trump nearly 200 times in his new memoir, “Promise Me, America”, repeatedly returning to the political rival whose return to power followed Biden’s withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race.The memoir, released on Wednesday, revisits revisits his four years in the White House, his legislative record, the Covid-19 pandemic, the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, the wars in Ukraine and Israel, and his decision to seek re-election in 2024 before withdrawing from the race.The Washington Post noted that Biden had initially sought to avoid drawing attention to Trump when he took office. Five years later, however, the Republican's name appears nearly 200 times in the memoir.The book, released almost two years after Biden left office, also offers him an opportunity to defend his decisions and revisit the pressure from fellow Democrats to abandon his re-election campaign after his debate performance against Trump in June 2024.The frequency of the references comes against the backdrop of Trump’s own repeated focus on his predecessor. Reuters reported in September that Trump had invoked Biden’s name nearly 900 times this year, averaging three mentions a day across speeches, public remarks and Truth Social posts.He blamed the former president for issues ranging from inflation and immigration to munitions shortages, even as Biden had largely withdrawn from public life.Biden makes no apology for seeking a second term, arguing that he believed he was best placed to defeat Trump.“The primaries sent no warning signs that I was in trouble,” he writes. “But that couldn’t derail the narrative setting in on my candidacy. That I was too old. That I was declining mentally.”Recalling the presidential debate in Atlanta, Biden says he had questioned his advisers about whether debating Trump was necessary.“It’s not that I was concerned about my ability to debate Donald Trump,” he writes. “It was that he was so prone to lying with abandon, bullying the moderators, violating the rules, whining about even a hint of fact checking, that I didn’t know whether there would be any value in my giving a public platform to this behavior.”Biden also acknowledges his stumble while discussing the federal deficit, when he said, “We finally beat Medicare,” instead of “We finally beat Big Pharma”, referring to his administration’s efforts to negotiate lower prescription drug prices.“Ironically, this historic achievement wouldn’t lift my candidacy. It would help to sink it,” he writes.He recalls senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urging him to leave the race, saying it was “personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me”.The Washington Post analysis noted that Trump appears more frequently in the memoir than other prominent figures. Vice president Kamala Harris is mentioned around 50 times, while former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi receives fewer than 30 mentions.Biden praises Harris's 2024 campaign, describing her as “a first-rate candidate” who “performed masterfully in her debate with President Trump”.He also criticises Trump over the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack and his pardons of those involved. Newsweek reported that the memoir also recalls a handwritten letter Trump left for Biden on the Resolute Desk before leaving office in January 2021. Biden describes the note as “beguiling”.The memoir revisits Biden’s defence of the Afghanistan withdrawal and his support for Israel, while acknowledging tensions with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “He and I could be direct with each other, but there wasn’t a ton of trust,” Biden writes, according to news agency AP.The memoir adds to the debate over Biden’s legacy, his decision to seek a second term and the political impact of Trump’s return to the White House.
Article Summary: Biden mentions Trump nearly 200 times in his new memoir, “Promise Me, America’ The book revisits revisits his four years in the White House, his legislative record, the Covid-19 pandemic, the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, the wars in Ukraine and Israel.

Article Title: ‘It just hits me right in the neck’: ‘Evil owl’ terrorises US state, multiple attacks reported
Article Text:
The string of attacks by the evil owl has been reported in Brookline, Massachusetts.

Residents describe sudden attacks by owl

Why could the owl be attacking people?

An aggressive owl has been attacking residents in a Massachusetts neighbourhood in the US, leaving at least a dozen people reporting strikes to their heads and necks. The attacks have been reported in Brookline, a town south of Boston, prompting local police to alert state wildlife officials and seek guidance on how to deal with the bird.The Brookline Police Department has received three or four calls about the owl swooping down on pedestrians and scratching them, according to a report by CBS Boston. Police have informed wildlife authorities about the incidents and are awaiting further instructions, Boston 25 News reported.Several residents have described being struck without warning while walking or running through the neighbourhood. Brookline News reporter Milena Fernsler, who was among those attacked, told PEOPLE that she was hit twice near her apartment on the Brookline-Brighton border.One of the victims, Taris Besse, told CBS Boston that the bird struck him on the neck while he was outside."Out of nowhere, it just hits me right in the neck. I heard it above me, so it definitely came right from the tree above me," Besse said.He subsequently went to the hospital and received rabies treatment as a precaution. Recalling his visit for a booster dose, Besse said a nurse recognised him as another victim of the owl attacks."For my first booster dose going back to the hospital, the nurse said, 'Oh, are you one of the other ones who got attacked by the owl?' Then I laughed," he told CBS Boston.Juliette Daily, another resident, told Boston 25 News that she was running along Dean Road when she felt something hit the top of her head. Initially believing it was a tree branch, she soon realised that a bird was responsible."It turned around and came back towards me. That time I actually ducked and it missed me, and it tried to go for a third pass," Daily recalled. She eventually ran across the street to escape the bird.Brookline News reporter Fernsler also described being struck twice. Recounting her experience, she said a "forceful whack" caused a sharp pain at the back of her head. She later spotted the owl perched on a telephone pole against the moonlit sky.Fernsler subsequently put up posters across the neighbourhood asking, "Have you been attacked by an owl?" in an effort to find other victims. She received around a dozen reports from people who said they had encountered the bird, according to Brookline News.The earliest reported incidents date back to last fall, with several attacks taking place within a short period around Halloween, Brookline News reported.Massachusetts is home to eight owl species, all of which are protected under state law, according to the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife).Although aggressive behaviour in owls is uncommon, the birds can become defensive when protecting a nearby nest, CBS Boston reported, citing MassWildlife.Police have contacted state wildlife officials for guidance on managing the situation as reports of attacks continue to emerge.
Article Summary: At least a dozen people have reported being struck by owl in Brookline, Massachusetts. Police have contacted state wildlife officials for guidance on how to deal with the bird. Massachusetts is home to eight owl species, all of which are protected under state law.

Article Title: Arkansas prosecutors moved to seize a man's home in a drug case, but an appeals court compared its $127,967 purchase price with his $2,500 fine and ruled the forfeiture unconstitutional
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Drug investigation led to a forfeiture case

Why the appeals court found the forfeiture excessive

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Forfeiture order reversed and dismissed

A man convicted of possessing cocaine with intent to deliver faced the loss of his Arkansas home after prosecutors sought to seize the property in connection with his drug offence. However, an appeals court has ruled that taking a house purchased for nearly $128,000 was an excessive punishment when the man had received a $2,500 fine and 10 years of supervised probation.In a November 18, 2026, decision available on Justia, the Arkansas Court of Appeals reversed and dismissed the forfeiture order against Richard Smith 's property. The court found that although the house had a sufficient connection to the drug offence to qualify for forfeiture under state law, taking it would violate the Eighth Amendment's protection against excessive fines because the value of the property was grossly disproportionate to the seriousness of the offence.On April 20, 2023, the state filed a notice of lis pendens and notice of forfeiture lien concerning Smith's property. A search of his home was conducted around April 23, during which officers discovered a safe containing multiple bags, 3.1626 grams of cocaine and several pills. Smith was subsequently arrested on drug-related charges. A warrant of seizure for forfeiture followed on April 27.Smith pleaded guilty on August 8, 2024, to possessing between 10 and 200 grams of cocaine with intent to deliver, a Class A felony, and possessing drug paraphernalia, a Class A misdemeanour.He was sentenced to 120 months of supervised probation, one day in jail with credit for time served, and a $2,500 fine.The state subsequently pursued the forfeiture of his house, arguing that the property had been used in connection with drug activity. At the August 14, 2025, forfeiture hearing, officers testified that they had observed increased traffic at the residence before the search. Some individuals leaving the property were later found carrying methamphetamine. However, the state crime laboratory report showed that cocaine was the only controlled substance recovered from the house that had been tested. Officers could not explain why the remaining substances had not been tested.Smith testified that the drugs were for personal use and acknowledged that he was a heavy drug user. Nevertheless, the circuit court found sufficient evidence to support forfeiture and ordered the property transferred to the Fifteenth Judicial District Prosecuting Attorney's Office.Smith challenged the forfeiture, arguing that the evidence connecting his home to drug sales was insufficient and that taking the property would violate the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause. The Arkansas Court of Appeals agreed with his constitutional argument, although it rejected his challenge to the connection between the property and the offence. It explained that state law allowed real estate to be forfeited when it was used to facilitate certain serious drug offences. Smith's conviction was sufficient to establish the required connection.However, the court emphasised that a punitive forfeiture must remain proportionate to the seriousness of the underlying offence. Citing the US Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Bajakajian, it explained that courts must compare the value of the property being forfeited with the gravity of the crime.The evidence showed that Smith had purchased the house for $127,967.82 on July 12, 2019. Even without accounting for any appreciation in its value over the following six years, forfeiture would amount to more than 51 times the $2,500 fine imposed on him and more than five times the $25,000 maximum fine authorised for a Class A felony under Arkansas law.The judges also considered the punishment already imposed. Although the offence carried a potential prison sentence of up to 40 years, Smith received supervised probation rather than a lengthy prison term. The court further noted that the drugs and paraphernalia were found inside a removable safe, with no evidence of additional controlled substances, scales or firearms elsewhere in the house. There was also no evidence that Smith himself had been found carrying methamphetamine or that his offence had caused direct harm.The appeals court concluded that the state's decision to take Smith's entire home went far beyond a proportionate punishment for his offence. It also referred to the Arkansas Constitution, which recognises the right to property as a fundamental protection.Accordingly, the court held that forfeiting the house was grossly disproportionate and violated the Eighth Amendment. It reversed the circuit court's forfeiture order and dismissed the case.The ruling makes clear that even when property has a sufficient connection to a criminal offence to qualify for forfeiture under state law, the government cannot automatically take it. When a forfeiture is punitive, its value must also be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence.
Article Summary: Richard Smith was convicted of possessing cocaine with intent to deliver. He received a $2,500 fine and 10 years of supervised probation. The state pursued the forfeiture of his house, arguing that the property had been used in connection with drug activity. The Arkansas Court of Appeals reversed and dismissed the forfeiture order against Smith's property.

Article Title: A year before Apollo 13’s oxygen tank exploded, NASA engineer Arturo Campos had drafted an emergency power plan; it helped bring the crew home
Article Text:
NASA engineer Arturo Campos, who had written an emergency power plan a year before Apollo 13’s launch. Image Credits: NASA

A plan nobody had tested

From a mechanic’s son to NASA engineer

Apollo 13 astronauts Fred Haise, Jack Swigert and James Lovell aboard the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima after splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Image Credits: NASA

Fifteen hours and a lifeboat

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More than one night of work

Imagine being woken at home by a phone call that changes everything. That's what happened to Arturo Campos on 13 April 1970. According to NASA's profile of Campos , he was sleeping when colleagues at the Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center, called him in. An oxygen tank on Apollo 13 had ruptured. Three astronauts were stranded in a damaged spacecraft about 320,000 km (200,000 miles) away from Earth. Campos was the engineer who had drawn up a plan for exactly this kind of emergency.The blast cut off electricity, light and water in the command module. The Moon landing was abandoned, and the top priority became getting James Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise home alive. Before the mission, the team had prepared a backup plan. This plan involved shifting the power from the lunar module, which was designed to land on the Moon, to the command module. The agency’s profile adds that the plan had never been tested. Campos was the electrical power subsystem manager of the lunar module. He went to the Mission Evaluation Room and rewrote the plan on the spot for the damaged spacecraft. NASA quotes him as saying he had written procedures for that situation a year before.Campos was born in Laredo, Texas, in 1934 to a Mexican-American family. At the time, it wasn't common for Hispanic students to go for engineering degrees. At first, Campos wasn't even aiming for college, thinking of becoming a car mechanic like his father. His high school chemistry and physics teacher, Josephine Baird, saw the potential in him and encouraged him to take classes while working at his father's garage. He attended Laredo Junior College and earned a degree in electrical engineering from the University of Texas in 1956. He later supervised aircraft maintenance at Kelly Air Force Base before joining NASA in the early 1960s. There, he became one of the go-to figures behind the electrical system of the Apollo lunar modules, including the one used for the first Moon landing in 1969.The plan took about 15 hours to carry out. Enough power moved from the lunar module to the emergency batteries in the command module to provide heat for the crew, get them home and allow them to land safely. It was part of a much larger rescue mission. As described by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center , mission control declared the command module mortally wounded less than two hours after Swigert’s transmission, with only 15 minutes of power left. The crew moved to the lunar module, which served as a lifeboat, and spent three and a half days there. Its provisions had been planned for two astronauts for one and a half days. Carbon dioxide levels became critical before the team managed to put square filters from the command module into round openings.With all the instruments turned off to conserve power, the temperature dropped to 38°F (3°C). The crew landed in the Pacific Ocean near Samoa on 17 April 1970.Campos is remembered as someone proud of his heritage. He was one of the few Mexican-American employees at Johnson, where most of the staff were white. He helped recruit more Hispanic workers to the space programme. He also helped start the League of United Latin American Citizens Council 660, a chapter of Mexican-American engineers at NASA that handed out scholarships to Hispanic students. In 1970, Richard Nixon awarded him, and other members of mission control, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Campos retired in 1980, continued consulting for Houston firms, and passed away in 2001 at age 66. His story shows how big rescues often begin with quiet planning long before anyone needs them.
Article Summary: Arturo Campos was the electrical power subsystem manager of the lunar module. He rewrote the plan on the spot for the damaged spacecraft. Campos retired in 1980, continued consulting for Houston firms, and passed away in 2001 at age 66. He was one of the few Mexican-American employees at Johnson.

Article Title: Apollo 12 was struck by lightning twice after launch; a year-old test helped John Aaron recognise the bad telemetry and tell the crew, “SCE to AUX”
Article Text:
Rain, dark clouds and two lightning strikes: A Moon-bound launch that went wrong within seconds (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

A smooth start that turned scary

Engineer John Aaron monitored the spacecraft’s power and life-support systems during the launch. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

The engineer who remembered

What the switch really did

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Back on track right away

On the morning of 14 November 1969, Apollo 12 lifted off against a dark, rainy sky. Less than a minute later, lightning struck the rocket. As NASA 's history article ‘ 50 Years Ago: Return to the Moon ’ explains, the rocket was struck twice, and a young engineer named John Aaron helped save the day. Apollo 12 carried Pete Conrad, Richard Gordon and Alan Bean on NASA's second moon landing mission. Aaron’s fix was a rarely used switch.It was an ambitious mission. Apollo 12 aimed for a pinpoint landing in the Ocean of Storms near the robotic craft Surveyor 3 that had been sitting there since 1967. Everything was going smoothly for the first 36 seconds after takeoff. Conrad himself described it as a lovely liftoff. Then things went horribly wrong. As the rocket was flying at 6,600 feet and passing through cloud cover, lightning struck. Conrad saw a bright flash, and then most of the spacecraft’s electronics went offline, including three fuel cells powering it. The data on the controllers’ screens in Mission Control turned into gibberish. The second strike, at about 52 seconds into the flight, disabled the spacecraft's guidance system.Fortunately, the Saturn V rocket that was controlling the launch kept working normally.Flight director Gerry Griffin turned to John Aaron, a young engineer at the console that monitored the spacecraft's electrical, environmental and communications systems. Aaron’s data had gone from normal to gibberish. But he remembered a test from a year earlier, when he had seen similar signals. He worked out that a unit called the Signal Conditioning Equipment, or SCE, had suffered some sort of upset. A switch, rarely used, had to be moved from its normal position to auxiliary. Aaron told Griffin, who then had astronaut Jerry Carr call it up to the crew. According to Johannes Kemppanen’s Apollo Flight Journal essay, ‘ More than SCE to AUX ,’ Carr sent the message one minute and 36 seconds into the flight. Conrad was puzzled, but Alan Bean recalled that the switch was on his panel. He flipped it, and within seconds Aaron reported good data.The SCE collects sensor readings and sends them to Mission Control. It has two internal power supplies. The essay explains that the strike probably took out the main power source. The transition to AUX made the device use the backup source, making the figures visible again. Aaron's quick action restored the telemetry. The essay also provides some additional details.The crew could still read key power gauges inside the cabin, and Mission Control could communicate with them via radio. Kemppanen adds that the loss of telemetry itself was not a reason to abort the flight. What the fix gave Mission Control, he notes, was just some extra confidence at a tense moment.Apollo 12 was in a near-circular orbit around the Earth about 11 and a half minutes after launch. For the next two and a half hours, the crew and Mission Control checked every system. Carr then informed the crew they were go for the burn to send them toward the Moon. Conrad joked that NASA needed to do a little more all-weather testing. Apollo 12 touched down on the Moon on 19 November 1969. The Flight Journal essay notes that the launch rules were changed afterwards so that no launch would be attempted in conditions where lightning was a possibility. Apollo 12 remained the only Apollo mission struck by lightning in flight. In the end, a year-old test, recalled under pressure, helped keep the mission on track.
Article Summary: Apollo 12 was the only Apollo mission struck by lightning in flight. A young engineer named John Aaron helped save the day. Aaron’s fix was a rarely used switch. Apollo 12 carried Pete Conrad, Richard Gordon and Alan Bean on NASA's second moon landing mission.

Article Title: Satellite images show western Nebraska before and after March 2026’s fires; the Morrill Fire burned more than 640,000 acres in a week, becoming one of the state’s largest recorded wildfires
Article Text:
Satellite images of western Nebraska, taken on 28 February and 29 March 2026, show the land before and after the fires. The burned ground appears as a large tan area. Image Credits: Lauren Dauphin/NASA Earth Observatory

What satellite saw

Aerial view of the Morrill Fire on March 14, 2026. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why the grass burned so fast

What was lost on the ground

Small problems have a way of turning into something much bigger than anyone expects. A wildfire in western Nebraska did just that in a matter of hours. On the afternoon of 12 March 2026, the fire started in Morrill County. NASA’s Earth Observatory reported that strong winds pushed the fire across the prairie about 110 kilometres (70 miles) in just 12 hours. The Morrill Fire then burned more than 640,000 acres (260,000 hectares) in one week. That made it the biggest wildfire in the state's history.NASA released the before-and-after view image as their Earth Observatory image of the day on 31 March 2026. It was made using two images captured by the VIIRS sensor on board the NOAA-21 satellite. These images show how grasslands of western Nebraska changed before and after multiple fires occurred there. The first image was captured on 28 February 2026, while the second image was taken on 29 March 2026. Both use false colour, which helps to distinguish burned land from unburned land. The grasslands near the North Platte River in the first image are shown in light green and brown colours. In the second image, a large tan patch appears, indicating that the land has been burned.The second image shows how the landscape changed in about one month. By 29 March, authorities reported that the Morrill Fire was fully contained. Crews were still working on two smaller fires to the northeast, called Ashby and Minor, which had started early on 26 March.The conditions were set long before the first flame was lit. On 20 March 2026, the National Interagency Fire Center issued an advisory for the Northern and Central Great Plains. In March, it said, extreme rates of fire spread were being driven by historically dry fuels. It also pointed to a snow drought that had left the grass dried out and standing upright, which allowed fire to move faster. Since mid-December, the weather had been warmer and windier than usual. Much of the region also received less than half of its normal precipitation over 90 days. The area of concern included western and southern South Dakota, eastern Wyoming and all but southeastern Nebraska.The advisory cautioned that winds above 35 miles per hour could allow fire to spread through grasslands at a speed of more than 3 to 5 miles per hour. Some wildfires in Nebraska had already exceeded 100,000 acres, and the forecast for the remaining days of March offered little hope for widespread moisture. Fire activity was also unusually high across the country in early 2026. NASA's write-up noted that as of 27 March, 15,436 fires had burned 1,510,973 acres nationwide, compared to a 10-year average of 9,195 fires that burned 664,792 acres over the same period.It also highlighted that the Great Plains were highly susceptible to fire in early 2026, with unusual fire behaviour for the time of year.News reports cited by NASA indicated that the fires affected large areas of ranch and pastureland. They destroyed homes, barns, fences and injured or killed livestock. The Morrill Fire also burned across much of the Crescent Lake National Wildlife Refuge in the Nebraska Sandhills, an area of grasslands, wetlands and dunes that migratory birds use. Still, there were reports of hundreds of thousands of sandhill cranes making their annual migration through the Platte River valley. Together, the images and the reports show just how quickly a fire can grow when the land is this dry.
Article Summary: NASA released the before-and-after view image as their Earth Observatory image of the day on 31 March 2026. It was made using two images captured by the VIIRS sensor on board the NOAA-21 satellite. The images show how grasslands of western Nebraska changed before and after multiple fires occurred there.
