Everyone hopes for a Christmas miracle, but for Marsha Hinman, a retired school teacher from Western New York, it came in the form of a stranger's simple act of kindness. Someone she had never met decided that her handwritten family history was too precious to leave behind. After finding the manuscript Hinman had lost at an airport, the stranger mailed it to an old address listed inside. Her family received it and, on Christmas, her children wrapped the long-lost manuscript and gave it to her as a surprise present! "I fell to the floor sobbing," Hinman told ABC News. Now, that's what you call a Christmas miracle!For nearly four decades, Marsha Hinman of Spencerport, New York, had been writing down her family's story. Hinman's husband, Dan, had a long battle with multiple sclerosis and died in 1999, just three months before their first grandchild was born. Dan never met any of the children who came after. Wanting them to know who their grandfather was, Hinman began putting their family's memories, struggles and milestones into a book. The project grew into a large, spiral-bound volume.“He never met any of his grandchildren,” Hinman told Rochester.“So I thought, ‘I've got to write something so they know who he was and the legacy he had and how much the Spencerport and Brockport community cared for us.’”Hinman was serious about the book. Her five children eventually had 16 grandchildren between them, and the manuscript kept growing with the family. Each chapter held another piece of a life that had branched out in ways she could not have planned when she started.Hinman took the book with her on a trip to Florida ahead of Thanksgiving 2019. She planned to finish a few pages at Punta Gorda Airport on the way home, near Fort Myers, where she had a little time to herself before the flight. She didn't really get the chance to finish the book. She boarded the plane, only to realise that the manuscript was not in her bag. It was still at the airport. She told a flight attendant that she had to go back for it. The crew told her she could not leave the plane.“This book is my life. It's my whole life. It's not just a book. It's like my memoirs,” Hinman protested.She contacted the airport, only to realise that the manuscript could have been lost forever. "I did everything I thought I could to get it back," she told WHAM. But it didn't happen, at least not yet. All she could do was pray. “Because I needed a miracle.”Miracles don't always happen the way we imagine them. For Marsha Hinman, this one arrived in the most unexpected way. Someone at the airport found the book, looked through its pages for a clue to who owned it and found an old address written inside.That stranger mailed the manuscript, along with a note, to that address in Spencerport. The family who lived there now had no connection to the Hinmans beyond the house. But the homeowner recognised what the package might mean and reached out to Hinman's son about it. He went to pick up the book.Hinman had no idea any of this was happening. She was still waiting for news she wasn't sure would come. And it came wrapped as a Christmas present.When Hinman pulled off the wrapping paper, she was over the moon. Her family, who had watched her search and pray, saw the moment her face changed.“I fell to the floor sobbing. And I'm crying and I couldn't stop. Article Title: A Frida Kahlo painting expected to sell for up to $3.5 million was withdrawn from a Christie’s auction in New York just hours before bidding, after questions emerged over its ownership and how it left
Article Text:
Why the painting’s ownership is being questioned

The disputed journey from Mexico to private collections

What Mexican authorities have said

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A rare painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo was withdrawn from a high-profile Christie’s auction in New York shortly before it was due to go under the hammer, following concerns over its ownership history and whether it had been legally removed from Mexico. The development, reported by Smithsonian Magazine and El País, has brought renewed attention to the fate of artworks from Kahlo’s historic collection and the responsibility of auction houses to establish their provenance before a sale. The painting, Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace), was created in 1952 and had been expected to fetch between $2.5 million and $3.5 million at Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale on November 17, 2026. Its withdrawal came after Mexican cultural authorities sought further information about its ownership and the circumstances surrounding its departure from the country.The controversy centres on the painting’s connection to Casa Azul, the Mexico City home where Kahlo was born, lived for much of her life and died in 1954. The house was later converted into the Frida Kahlo Museum. According to the group Defendamos la Colección Gelman, the painting appears in an inventory prepared by Kahlo’s husband, fellow artist Diego Rivera, in 1957, when arrangements were made to preserve the couple’s belongings for the Mexican public.Rivera had intended the Casa Azul collection to remain a cultural legacy for the country.The group’s concerns are supported by Pedro Diego Alvarado, Rivera’s grandson, who has also placed the painting among the works and possessions kept at Kahlo’s studio in Casa Azul. The questions surrounding the artwork gained momentum after Hilda Trujillo, former director of the Frida Kahlo Museum, raised concerns in 2025 about discrepancies between the museum’s historical inventory and the artworks that were eventually accounted for. Her research pointed to several paintings and other works that appeared to have entered private collections, including Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. Trujillo also questioned how these works had left the museum’s collection and who had authorised their transfer.The painting’s movements over the decades have become central to the investigation. Mexican authorities initially maintained that the artwork had left the country in 1952, when it was taken to Vienna, Austria, for the Congress of the Peoples for Peace. The painting was created in connection with the gathering, which brought together artists, writers and intellectuals advocating peace.However, its subsequent history has raised questions. Christie’s records indicate that the painting returned to Mexico in 1953 and was displayed at Kahlo’s first solo exhibition in April that year, held at the Galería de Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City.Historical accounts also suggest that Rivera and his daughter, architect Ruth Rivera Marín, took the painting to Europe, as Kahlo’s deteriorating health prevented her from travelling. The artwork’s next documented public appearances came decades later. It featured in an exhibition in Madrid and Barcelona in 1997 and was subsequently included in a touring exhibition in Japan between 2003 and 2004.By 1988, however, the painting had already been identified in records as belonging to a private collection. It was later offered through a New York gallery before appearing at Sotheby’s in 2020, eventually entering the hands of a private collector. The gap between its return to Mexico in 1953 and its later appearance in private ownership is one of the central issues that investigators are seeking to clarify.Mexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL) has requested documentation from Christie’s to establish the painting’s provenance and legal ownership. The institute is also coordinating with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museum Trust, whose trustee is the Bank of Mexico. The legal position is particularly important. In 1984, Kahlo’s entire artistic output was declared an artistic monument under Mexican law. While the designation does not prohibit the domestic sale of her paintings, it restricts their permanent export from Mexico.INBAL’s initial position was that the painting had left the country before the 1984 decree came into effect. However, the documented return for Kahlo’s 1953 exhibition has complicated the question of when it actually left Mexico permanently. The Frida Kahlo Museum has confirmed that the painting is included in an ongoing investigation involving several artworks. Authorities are examining the available documentation as they seek to establish the circumstances surrounding the pieces’ ownership and movement.Christie’s subsequently confirmed that the decision to withdraw the painting was taken in agreement with its seller to allow further research. The auction house has indicated that it hopes to offer the work for sale at a later date, although no fresh auction date has been announced. For now, the painting remains at the centre of a wider debate about the preservation of Mexico’s artistic heritage, the protection of museum collections and the documentation required when historically significant works enter the international art market.
Article Summary: Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace) was created in 1952. Mexican authorities initially maintained that the artwork had left the country in 1952, when it was taken to Vienna, Austria. Christie’s records indicate that the painting returned to Mexico in 1953. It featured in an exhibition in Madrid and Barcelona in 1997 and was subsequently included in a touring exhibition in Japan between 2003 and 2004. By 1988, the painting had already been identified in records as belonging to a private collection.

Article Title: Why solutions sometimes make the problem worse? Experts debate at Harvard
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On October 18 at Harvard Medical School, about 110 Iranian scientists, engineers, founders and investors spent an hour on a question that sounds simple: why do well-intentioned decisions so often make a problem worse?The discussion was the centerpiece of the third 2See Summit, organized by Mehrzad Sajjadi and Saleh Dadkhahipour, hosts of the Persian-language 2See Podcast. It followed summits at Stanford University in July and the University of Southern California in August. The organizers say more than 300 people attended the three events.As at the earlier summits, Sajjadi and Dadkhahipour opened with a live recording of the podcast instead of a conventional panel. Their guests were Hazhir Rahmandad, the Schussel Family Professor of Management Science and a professor of system dynamics at the MIT Sloan School of Management, and Mohammad Jalali, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School based at the MGH Institute for Technology Assessment. Both work in system dynamics, a field that models how the parts of a complex system feed back on one another over time.The two professors walked through cases from forest fire management, hospital operations, addiction treatment and health policy in which a fix aimed at the visible symptom ended up strengthening the underlying cause. The conversation then moved to artificial intelligence. AI can help decision-makers test a policy before committing to it, the guests argued, but a model handed a poorly framed problem will return a polished answer to the wrong question.They also took up the future of work, Iran's demographic window, the distance between researchers and policymakers, and declining social trust."Most of us are trained to solve the problem in front of us," Sajjadi said. "Systems thinking asks what your solution does to everything around it. That applies to a health policy, a startup or an AI model.""The distance between the people who study a problem and the people who decide on it came up again and again," Dadkhahipour said.After the recording, the summit moved into a networking session. Attendees worked at companies and universities including Microsoft, MIT, Pfizer, Moderna and Fidelity Investments, though none of these organizations was involved in the event. Where the Stanford audience leaned toward AI laboratories and Silicon Valley startups, the Boston room added a large contingent from biotechnology and pharmaceuticals.The second summit was held at USC in Los Angeles on August 22 with more than 100 attendees. That live episode featured Kiana Aran, an associate professor of bioengineering and medicine at UC San Diego and co-founder of the graphene biosensor company Cardea Bio, and Salman Avestimehr, a Dean's Professor at USC and inaugural director of the USC-Amazon Center on Trustworthy AI. They discussed the meeting point of electronics and biology, automated laboratories, AI systems that propose hypotheses and design experiments, and how to tell when university research is ready to become a company.The series began on July 18 at Stanford, where nearly 120 people heard the hosts connect Cold War deterrence theory to the contest between open and closed frontier AI models.Dadkhahipour earned his MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business and is pursuing a Master in Public Administration at Harvard Kennedy School. Sajjadi is pursuing an MBA and a master's in computer science at Stanford and a master's in biotechnology at Harvard. Before Stanford he was a robotics engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and founded nFlux, an AI computer-vision company focused on manufacturing, which he exited to Invisible AI in 2025.The two started 2See in November 2025 from their dorm rooms at Stanford and Harvard. The show has released 48 episodes and, according to the hosts, has more than 300,000 followers across platforms. The name 2See is pronounced like "Tusi" in Persian, a reference to the 13th-century Iranian polymath Nasir al-Din Tusi.The word also means "grey" in Persian and reads as "to see" in English."In every city we heard the same thing: people knew the names in the room but had never met," Dadkhahipour said. "Silicon Valley, Los Angeles and Boston all have deep Iranian talent. What was missing was a reason to be in the same room."The organizers say a fourth summit is planned for New York. The Harvard conversation with Rahmandad and Jalali was released as episode 46 of the podcast.
Article Summary: Iranian scientists, engineers, founders and investors met in Boston for the third 2See Summit. The event followed summits at Stanford University in July and the University of Southern California in August. The organizers say more than 300 people attended the three events. A fourth summit is planned for New York.

Article Title: A Florida State University student joined a bone marrow registry in 2019; her donation saved a 7-year-old boy's life, and years later, he finally met the woman who gave him a second chance
Article Text:
A student's 2019 bone marrow registry sign-up led to a life-saving match

Seven-year-old Samuel was diagnosed with a rare immune disorder

Donor and recipient meet for the first time at Los Angeles gala

Another donor-recipient pair reunites at the event

How the Gift of Life Marrow Registry connects donors with patients

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A decision made during a university recruitment drive in 2019 eventually brought 27-year-old Hope Miller face to face with seven-year-old Samuel Moore, whose life she helped save. Miller had joined the Gift of Life Marrow Registry while studying at Florida State University, unaware of who might one day need her help. A few years later, she was identified as a match for Samuel, who had been diagnosed with a rare inherited immune disorder at the age of three. She agreed to donate her bone marrow, giving him an opportunity to undergo a life-saving transplant. The two finally met at a charity gala in Los Angeles on November 16, 2026, turning an anonymous act of generosity into an emotional reunion.Miller joined the Gift of Life Marrow Registry in 2019 during a donor recruitment drive held at Florida State University. By registering, she made herself available to be matched with a patient who needed a bone marrow or blood stem cell transplant.The match eventually came in the form of Samuel, who was just three years old when he was diagnosed with DOCK8 deficiency, a rare inherited immune disorder. The condition affects the body's ability to fight infections and can leave patients vulnerable to severe and potentially life-threatening illnesses.When Miller learnt that she was a match for the young boy, she agreed to donate. She said she made the decision after speaking with her family and considering how she would feel if someone close to her needed such help. Learning that the recipient was a little boy also made the decision particularly personal, as she has brothers.DOCK8 deficiency is a genetic condition that affects the immune system, leaving those diagnosed with it at risk of serious and recurring infections. Children with the disorder can experience viral, bacterial and fungal infections, along with other complications.Samuel's diagnosis at the age of three meant that his family had to navigate a difficult medical journey. His mother, Christy Moore, said they were relieved to learn that a bone marrow transplant could save his life.She also spoke about the uncertainty of depending on an unknown person to make the decision to donate. The family was grateful that someone who had never met Samuel was willing to help him.Miller's donation provided the marrow needed for Samuel's transplant, offering him a chance at a healthier future.The long-awaited meeting took place during Gift of Life Marrow Registry's One Huge Night gala at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel in Los Angeles on November 16, 2026. Miller and Samuel came face to face for the first time at the event, which brought together donors, transplant recipients, supporters and advocates.Miller said she had hoped that if anyone in her own family ever needed a donation, another person would be willing to step forward. Her decision to join the registry eventually connected her with a child whose life depended on finding a compatible donor.For Samuel's family, the meeting offered an opportunity to thank the woman whose willingness to donate had helped make his treatment possible.The gala also witnessed another emotional reunion between donor Max Mandel and 32-year-old Juan Santoyo of Wasco, California.Mandel, a Los Angeles native now living in New York City, had joined the registry in 2015 while studying in Jerusalem. He later donated blood stem cells to Santoyo, helping save his life after he was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.Santoyo was a husband and father when he became ill, and his wife was pregnant with their second child at the time. His reunion with Mandel brought together two people whose lives had become connected through the donation process.Unlike Miller, who donated bone marrow, Mandel provided peripheral blood stem cells, another method used in transplants.Gift of Life Marrow Registry is a US-based nonprofit organisation established in 1991. It works to facilitate bone marrow and blood stem cell transplants for patients with conditions including leukaemia, lymphoma and inherited immune disorders.People can register as potential donors through a cheek-swab process that allows their tissue type to be recorded. When a patient needs a transplant, the registry is searched for a compatible match. Further testing is conducted before a donation can proceed.Depending on the patient's medical needs, a donor may provide blood stem cells or bone marrow. Miller and Mandel's stories illustrate how people who have never met can become connected through a decision to register and help someone in need.
Article Summary: Hope Miller, 27, joined the Gift of Life Marrow Registry in 2019. A few years later, she was identified as a match for seven-year-old Samuel Moore. Samuel had been diagnosed with a rare inherited immune disorder at the age of three. Miller agreed to donate her bone marrow, giving him a chance at a healthier future. The two finally met at a charity gala in Los Angeles on November 16, 2026.

Article Title: Sikh grandmother's deportation to India inspires US bill to protect long-term immigrants
Article Text:
How a Sikh grandmother's deportation to India sparked a US immigration bill

What does the bill propose

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The deportation of a 73-year-old Sikh grandmother to India after nearly three decades in the US has prompted four California lawmakers to introduce a bill in the US Congress seeking protection for long-term immigrant residents.The proposed legislation, called the Protect Our Neighbours Act, was introduced by Congressman John Garamendi. It was inspired by the case of Harjit Kaur, a resident of the San Francisco Bay Area who was detained and deported by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last year.Representatives Lateefah Simon, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas have also backed the bill.Simon said the legislation would give people like Kaur, who had worked in her district for decades, a fair chance to move beyond a final deportation order and continue building their lives in the US, where they have homes and families.Garamendi said Kaur had no criminal record and had regularly reported to ICE every six months for more than 13 years before she was detained and deported.He criticised her detention and deportation, saying it was another example of how ICE's actions under US President Donald Trump had disrupted the lives of thousands of people and their families across the country.According to the American Immigration Council, around 1.19 million people with final deportation orders remain in the US.Many have spent years working, raising families and building their lives in the country.Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security and ICE have stepped up action against people with final deportation orders, including long-term residents who have regularly complied with immigration check-ins.The Protect Our Neighbours Act seeks to make final deportation orders expire 10 years after they are issued.Under the proposal, an immigration judge could renew an expired order at the request of the Homeland Security Secretary. However, the government would have to provide clear and convincing evidence of significant reasons for the delay that were not related to administrative or funding problems. It would also have to present new evidence showing that renewing the order was in the public interest.The bill would also allow people whose deportation orders have expired and have not been renewed to apply for lawful immigration status if they qualify. To be eligible, they must have lived continuously in the US for at least 10 years and must not have been convicted of an offence punishable by more than one year in prison.The government would not be allowed to renew their deportation orders while such an application was pending.A separate provision would allow certain people who have lived in the US for a long time despite having outstanding deportation orders to apply for permanent residence, depending on the immigration grounds involved.
Article Summary: The Protect Our Neighbours Act was introduced by Congressman John Garamendi. It was inspired by the case of Harjit Kaur, a resident of the San Francisco Bay Area who was detained and deported by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last year.

United Nations high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan , raising concerns over his reported deteriorating health and detention conditions. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case.In an interview with Christiane Amanpour on CNN, Turk said Khan's release could help build confidence between the government and the opposition.“I call for Imran Khan’s release. I call for his proper treatment, and I actually call for de-escalation. We need to diffuse the political tensions that are around this case, which means that a confidence-building measure between the opposition and the government could be his immediate release,” Turk said.His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister, who remains in detention at Adiala Jail. Earlier, Khan's son Kasim Khan appealed to the international community to intervene, accusing Pakistan's military leadership, headed by Army chief Asim Munir, of violence and repression.“Munir and his regime will not listen to reason. They kill, abduct and torture at will.It is time the world acted, before they kill my father, the rightful, democratically elected leader of Pakistan,” Kasim wrote in a post on X.Amnesty International has also called for urgent intervention, citing restrictions on Khan's access to family members, healthcare and legal representation.The organisation said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family since December 2025, apart from two meetings with his sister in August 2026. It also said he had not been permitted to speak to his sons over the telephone since March 2026.Amnesty expressed concern over his reported solitary confinement and isolation from human contact, warning that the conditions could affect his physical and mental health. It also flagged reports of severe blood pressure complications and alleged that authorities had denied him access to independent doctors despite an August Supreme Court order directing that he be taken to a private hospital.The organisation also raised concerns over the health of Khan's wife, Bushra Bibi, alleging that she had been denied adequate treatment for an eye condition that could lead to vision loss.Amnesty said the treatment of the detained couple violated Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which requires authorities to treat people deprived of their liberty with humanity and respect.The organisation also called for the release of Khan's sister Aleema Khan, who remains detained at Kot Lakhpat Prison in Lahore. It said three of his sisters were detained on September 20 and 21 in connection with a planned Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf march to Islamabad.Khan had also issued an open letter to Pakistan's top judges on November 16, seeking urgent medical treatment and implementation of court orders. He alleged that he had been held in “torturous solitary confinement for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025.
Article Summary: U.N. high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case. His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister.

Article Title: 'Bloodshed in Karachi, Hyderabad': Why Bilawal Bhutto is opposing plan to redraw Pakistan's map
Article Text:
What is Pakistan's province-redrawing plan that has Bilawal Bhutto warning of bloodshed?

Why is Pakistan considering more provinces

Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces, warning against any attempt to split Sindh by force.He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad, Pakistan-based Geo TV reported.The proposal to redraw Pakistan's political map has reportedly found support among several leaders in the country's power corridors, including army chief Asim Munir and defence minister Khawaja Asif Speaking at an event at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal said any forced division of the province would create social divisions and push ordinary people towards violence, Geo TV reported.“If the province is divided by force, society will be divided, it will lead to enmity, ordinary people will take up arms, and the bloodshed will not be limited to a single death,” he said.The remarks come amid discussions in Pakistan about reorganising its administrative structure by dividing its four provinces into smaller units. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces or reorganise the country into as many as 160 smaller administrative units to address governance challenges.The proposal has gained support from some senior ministers, but faces opposition from political parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh, where the Bhutto-Zardari family and the PPP have a strong political base.Bilawal said the PPP was not opposed to creating new provinces but insisted that any such move must follow the wishes of the people and the constitutional process.“The PPP supports the creation of provinces in line with the wishes of the people, the Constitution and the law. Where we are opposing, it is over force and coercion. We do not want division through force,” he said.He also questioned suggestions that a referendum could be used to decide the issue, saying the Constitution already provided a procedure for creating new provinces.“If you are looking for an unconstitutional method, how can the PPP be with you?” he asked.Bilawal further said referendums in Pakistan's history had been used for undemocratic purposes. “It is not about a referendum, it is about intent,” he said.The proposal to increase the number of provinces from four to as many as 12 has gained momentum, with supporters arguing that smaller administrative units could improve governance and public services.Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has backed the idea, saying the country's growing population requires smaller provinces for more efficient administration.Speaking to Geo News, Asif said Pakistan could consider creating 12 provinces, provided their boundaries were based on administrative needs rather than linguistic, ethnic or political considerations.However, the proposal faces a major political challenge, with no consensus among leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.

He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces.

Article Title: $135 billion in debt, still getting loans: Who is keeping Pakistan afloat, and why
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and chief of defence forces Asim Munir (Reuters file photo)

What World Bank’s International Debt Report says about Pakistan

Pakistan’s economic challenges

China: Pakistan’s ‘all-weather’ friend

Why financial institutions continue lending to Pakistan

Can Pakistan actually repay its debt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens if creditors stop lending to Pakistan

The World Bank ’s International Debt Report 2026 paints a stark picture of Pakistan’s growing external debt burden, showing that, as of 2025, Islamabad’s external debt had nearly doubled from its 2015 level.According to the report, Pakistan’s external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015, marking a 97% increase in just 10 years.Pakistan's mounting external debt presents a curious contradiction. Its economy continues to struggle, and its dependence on foreign financing remains substantial. Yet, despite these vulnerabilities, money continues to flow into the country from some of the world's most influential governments and financial institutions.The question, therefore, is not simply why Islamabad keeps borrowing, but why its creditors continue lending to a country whose ability to generate sufficient foreign exchange and meet its repayment obligations remains a source of concern.The $135.1 billion, which Pakistan owed as external debt, was up 4% from $129.9 billion in 2024. Of the 2025 debt, around $107.1 billion was public and publicly guaranteed debt, while the remainder included private-sector and short-term external obligations.Of Pakistan’s public and publicly guaranteed debt, nearly $57 billion is owed to multilateral creditors, while bilateral creditors account for over $42 billion, with the remainder owed to private creditors.Among individual creditors, China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. It is followed by the World Bank, with $19.2 billion, and the Asian Development Bank, with $16.83 billion, among other creditors.The report also highlighted the burden of debt repayments on Pakistan’s economy. In 2025, Islamabad spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt, while total external debt stood at 34% of Gross National Income.The report, therefore, highlights the challenge facing Islamabad: managing its growing external debt while ensuring that its economy generates enough foreign exchange to meet repayment obligations.Continued lending does not necessarily mean Pakistan’s economy is healthy. Nor does its growing debt burden mean the country is on the verge of default.The latest economic indicators present a mixed picture.The World Bank estimates that Pakistan’s economy grew by 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% in the previous financial year. The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP, while the current account recorded a small deficit of 0.1% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also reported that Pakistan’s gross foreign exchange reserves had risen to approximately $21.5 billion by the end of September 2025.These gains, however, are offset by continued economic challenges. Economic growth has not generated enough jobs for Pakistan’s growing workforce. About 3.5 million people enter the workforce every year, yet unemployment stood at 7% in 2024. While nearly 18 million new jobs have been created since 2018, most have been informal, low-paid or self-employment opportunities.Poverty, too, has increased, with the rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. An estimated 70 million Pakistanis are now living in poverty.The future outlook also remains challenging. The World Bank projected Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.8% in FY27, a marginal increase from the estimated 3.7% growth in FY26. Headline inflation was expected to rise to 8.2% in FY27 before easing to around 7%.The data therefore highlights the economic pressures Pakistan faces and is expected to confront in the coming years.China being Pakistan’s largest individual creditor is perhaps unsurprising. Beijing and Islamabad are, after all, each other’s “all-weather friends.”China’s investment in Pakistan has largely been channelled through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the flagship project of Beijing’s ambitious Belt and Road Initiative. Under CPEC, Chinese investment in Pakistan is estimated at $62 billion over a period of 15 years.Another important feature of this economic relationship is loan rollover, under which a creditor extends the repayment period of existing loans instead of demanding immediate repayment. China has continued to roll over existing loans to Pakistan, providing Islamabad temporary relief from its foreign currency obligations without reducing its overall debt.With Pakistan struggling to repay its Chinese loans, what explains Beijing's willingness to not only continue providing financial support to Islamabad but also roll over existing loans?Sushant Sareen, senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation and an expert on Pakistan, attributed Beijing's continued support to the “strategic relationship” between the two countries.“It’s not just about an economic relationship between them. I think one of the reasons why the Chinese keep bailing Pakistan out and give them money is because of the strategic relationship that exists between them,” Sareen told The Times of India.Even CPEC, he added, was China’s plan to “prop up” Pakistan’s economy and make it more efficient and productive.Ultimately, the question is whether Pakistan can generate enough foreign exchange to service its growing debt, even with continued support from China.That Beijing is Islamabad’s largest creditor comes as little surprise. However, multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank also continue to play an important role in financing Pakistan.Since joining the IMF in 1950, Pakistan has received around two dozen bailout packages. Most recently, in October, the IMF agreed to release another $1.21 billion under its ongoing loan and sustainability programmes, subject to Executive Board approval.In a recent YouTube interview, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath was asked why the lender continues to bail out Pakistan despite concerns over its ability to repay its loans.Gopinath explained that the IMF’s role is to help countries facing economic crises and that it cannot simply walk away from them.She also emphasised that the IMF's decisions are taken by its member countries, including India. The decision to extend a loan, therefore, rests with the membership rather than the IMF's management.Sareen echoed this view.“Pakistan is a member of the IMF. It is the IMF’s job to bail out countries which are facing balance of payments problems,” he said.He, however, pointed out that political considerations could also influence the IMF's lending decisions.“India holds slightly over 2% vote share and that's not big enough to veto the loan. The Americans with 16% or 17% stake can actually do that, because with 15% you can veto any IMF loan. And clearly the Americans don't want to turn the screws on the Pakistanis. So, yes, to some extent it is a political decision to give money to Pakistan,” he argued.Sareen noted, however, that overall, the IMF largely operates within its economic mandate.Taken together, Islamabad's repeated reliance on the IMF underlines the extent to which its economy depends on external financial support.Pakistan's total external debt of around $135 billion does not mean the entire amount is due for repayment immediately. The debt has accumulated over several years, with repayments spread across different periods.The extent of Pakistan's reliance on fresh borrowing is evident from the figures. In FY26, it received $16.16 billion in external loans, while repaying around $14.44 billion in external public debt, including $11.20 billion in principal and $3.24 billion in interest, according to the ministry of economic affairs.The key question, therefore, is whether Islamabad can generate enough foreign exchange to meet these repayment obligations while managing its other economic needs.Sareen argued that the bigger challenge for Pakistan was not repaying its entire debt, but servicing it — having enough foreign exchange to meet repayment and interest obligations as they fall due.“Pakistans' problem is that they're not earning the kind of foreign exchange they require to service that debt. And the debt which they're taking on is increasing virtually every year. But for now, they're managing to tide it over. They managed to avoid default, but at a very high price,” he said.The challenge for Islamabad, therefore, is not just to keep securing loans, but to build an economy capable of meeting its repayment obligations without repeatedly relying on external support.Pakistan is often described as a country facing economic collapse and the risk of disintegration. Its continued dependence on external financing raises an important question: what would happen if lenders stopped extending fresh loans to Islamabad?The withdrawal of support from its lenders would not automatically push Pakistan into default or close to disintegration. Rather, it would face severe economic difficulties.Sareen warned that a default could trigger severe economic hardship, with Pakistan potentially spending three to four years trying to stabilise its economy and regain access to the international financial system. During this period, it could struggle to maintain imports and deal with foreign exchange shortages.But Pakistan continues to stay afloat — with support from international institutions, as well as countries whose financial assistance is shaped by strategic interests. Lending decisions also have a political dimension, with the interests and influence of powerful member countries playing a role.For now, creditors continue to extend financial support, even as concerns over Islamabad's ability to repay its debt persist.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015. China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. Pakistan spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt.

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. He will be killed in this cell if he remains there any longer without proper treatment," the brothers said.They also alleged that prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him."I mean, we've been saying this for months. They're torturing him in the cell. It's physical and mental torture. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. But none of that has been implemented. And his health has just continued to deteriorate," they said."His blood pressure is now dangerously high, at about 193, I think. So he needs to be treated at a private hospital immediately," they added.The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi. He said his blood pressure had risen sharply and doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.In the letter, released by his party and lawyer Salman Safdar, Khan also alleged that authorities had failed to implement the earlier hospital transfer order. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. The government has also rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.
Article Summary: Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan accuse authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail. They allege that he is being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care. Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife.

Article Title: Former Pakistan army officer is new BLA chief
Article Text:
BLA appoints ex-Pakistan Army Captain as chief (file photo)

In a major organisational shift, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has elevated its senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Sources said his elevation carried symbolic weight given his past as a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment.In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians, and joined Aslam Baloch’s BLA, leaving the military brass flummoxed. Prior to assuming the top role, Gul served on the command council and led the Majeed Brigade, BLA’s operational wing which specialises in suicide bombings.Having graduated as a battalion senior major, Gul previously held military postings in Kotli in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir as well as North and South Waziristan, where he took part in military operations.The announcement also dispels earlier reports from the Pakistani military, which had declared Gul dead last year, a claim BLA didn’t validate. Adding a sensitive dynamic to the situation, sources indicate that Gul’s younger brother currently serves as a Major in the Pakistan army’s Signals Corps. Observers suggest that having a former military officer at the helm amplifies narratives of internal disillusionment among security personnel regarding state crackdowns and civilian casualties in Balochistan.The leadership transition, confirmed through a statement from group spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch on Nov 14, follows a unanimous vote by the outfit’s senior command council. The move comes just days after the announcement that Bashir Zeb was stepping down as chief.There was also uncertainty surrounding Zeb’s successor after the group said last week that Zeb was transferring all powers to the command council. While pro-Pak military social media accounts circulated rumours of Zeb having been poisoned by a confidante and being killed in Afghanistan, sources described them as false.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) elevate senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Gul is a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment. In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians.

Article Title: Redrawing Pakistan: Ministers back 12-province plan but political, constitutional hurdles remain
Article Text:
Pakistan's 12-province proposal gains momentum as senior ministers back restructuring (Representative Image)

What the proposed 12-province map could look like

Political consensus remains the biggest hurdle

What the Constitution requires

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better governance. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. Speaking to Geo News, he said the country could consider creating 12 provinces, provided the boundaries were drawn on administrative rather than linguistic, ethnic or political grounds.“If there is a proposal for 12 provinces, then make it 12,” Asif said, adding that new units should not be created to serve “language, ethnicity or political interests”.Pakistan’s interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also revived the debate, suggesting a referendum to gauge public opinion on the contentious issue. His remarks have fuelled speculation that powerful quarters favour a broader restructuring of Pakistan's administrative map, with reports pointing to a possible constitutional exercise in 2027.No formal roadmap, however, has been announced. The proposed number of provinces, their boundaries and the process for creating them remain undecided.One proposal reported in Pakistani media envisages dividing Punjab into four provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan into three each, and Sindh into two. The plan could involve a nationwide referendum and a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, although neither has been confirmed as an approved government initiative.Supporters argue that the existing arrangement concentrates too much administrative and financial authority in provincial capitals leaving smaller cities and districts dependent on decisions taken far away.Asif has questioned whether federal funds transferred to provincial governments are reaching local institutions, arguing that decentralisation could bring decision-making and resources closer to communities. Advocates of the proposal say smaller provinces would make public services more accessible and help address uneven development.But the debate is not only about the size of administrative units. It also raises questions about whether creating more provinces would improve governance without stronger local governments and greater financial autonomy for districts.The proposal has exposed differences within the ruling coalition itself. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), led by Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, has firmly opposed any division of Sindh, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has yet to settle on a formal position.The two parties are coalition partners in the federal government. The PML-N has said it will announce its position if the matter comes before Parliament, despite some of its leaders backing the creation of smaller provinces.A cabinet member in the Shehbaz Sharif government said reaching agreement would be difficult without the support of the major political parties.The issue has also prompted speculation about a possible understanding between the government and the main opposition, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). PML-N leader and former federal minister Khawaja Saad Rafique has suggested that the establishment could offer relief to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in return for PTI's support for the proposed constitutional changes. There has been no confirmation of such a deal.Smaller parties have also entered the debate. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its demand for new administrative units in Sindh, while Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain has called for new provinces to be considered through consultation and in the national interest.The Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party has backed the proposal on administrative grounds, while Jamaat-i-Islami has argued that the creation of new provinces should go hand in hand with strengthening local governments.Even if political parties agree on the broad idea, redrawing provincial boundaries would require a demanding constitutional process.Under Article 239 of Pakistan's Constitution, an amendment requires the support of at least two-thirds of the total membership of both houses of Parliament. If it changes the limits of an existing province, it must also secure the backing of at least two-thirds of the total membership of that province's assembly.That gives provincial parties considerable leverage over any proposed division.A nationwide referendum is not an automatic constitutional requirement for creating provinces. Any such exercise would need its own legal and constitutional basis, and Parliament could not simply be bypassed in deciding the process or framing the questions put to voters.Following a meeting between Pakistan’s president Asif Ali Zardari and prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday, a senior government official told news agency PTI that the two leaders had agreed to adhere strictly to the constitutional provisions governing the creation of new provinces. They also agreed that any proposed referendum would require parliamentary approval.Former federal information minister Muhammad Ali Durrani has meanwhile launched a campaign for the restoration of Bahawalpur province and the creation of 11 other smaller administrative units.For now, the proposal remains a subject of political debate rather than an agreed government plan. Any move to redraw the map would require agreement on boundaries, resources, parliamentary representation and the future of provincial institutions — as well as the constitutional numbers to make it happen.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.

Article Title: 24 militants, four soldiers killed in separate clashes in Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
(Photo credit: IANS)

At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, the Pakistan Army said on Saturday, PTI reported.The army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki.During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants, including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition, the military said.The army said the militants used armed quadcopters to target military vehicles on patrol. The attack killed Major Omer Minhas Nasir and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan.Separately, security forces conducted operations against militant hideouts in Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, 16 militants were killed in the engagements. Twelve were killed in an operation in Ali Khel, while two each were killed in Mir Ali and Datta Khel.Two soldiers, Havildar Asmat Ali and Naik Aftab Ali, were killed during the operations. The ISPR said both soldiers fought bravely and laid down their lives in the line of duty. It added that the operations had dealt a major blow to the militant network.Weapons and ammunition were recovered from the slain militants, who, according to the military, were involved in several terrorist activities, including the killing of civilians.Pakistan's federal government uses the term 'Fitna al-Khawarij' for militants belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Article Summary: At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants. The Pakistan Army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts.

At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, a security official reported on Friday.The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district, along the N-25 national highway. The vehicle struck a Frontier Corps (FC) checkpoint, according to a security official quoted by PTI.The three militants killed in the attack included the bomber, while two civilians also died. The injured included FC personnel, the official said. However, Dawn, quoting Balochistan police, reported that at least 16 people were injured, including three members of the border forces.The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing, identifying the suicide attacker as Osama Shahwani and saying he had joined the organisation in 2022.A security official, however, said Shahwani's name had appeared in a missing-persons case in 2024. The official alleged that the incident pointed to the BLA's recruitment of young Baloch men and its attempts to mislead authorities about their whereabouts.The injured were shifted to nearby hospitals for treatment. Security agencies are investigating the attack and the circumstances surrounding the bomber's links to the insurgent group.
Article Summary: At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province. The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing. The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district.

Article Title: Pakistani teen mauled to death by tigress released from cage for TikTok video shoot
Article Text:
Pakistani teenager mauled to death after tigress freed for TikTok video in Lahore (Image source: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 19-year-old Pakistani teenager was mauled to death by a tigress after it was let out of its cage for a TikTok video shoot.The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. He was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment on Wednesday, according to local reports.Police identified the arrested farm owner as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure. The animal subsequently lost control and attacked the worker, police said.The incident also triggered an investigation into an alleged attempt to conceal the circumstances of the death. Police said efforts were made to portray the attack as an incident involving a dog rather than a big cat. The animal has since been handed over to wildlife authorities.Authorities are examining whether the farm had the necessary permits to keep the animal and whether adequate safety measures were in place at the facility. A case has been registered and investigations into possible negligence are under way.In a statement, Lahore Police said that the pursuit of social media content could not come at the cost of human life. It said all aspects of the alleged negligence and the attempt to conceal the attack would be investigated.There has been some confusion in initial media reports over whether the animal was a tiger or a lion. Lahore Police's statement described it as a tigress.
Article Summary: The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure.

Article Title: Imran Khan-Asim Munir deal? Sisters' release from jail, hospital visit spark buzz in Pakistan
Article Text:
Release of Imran Khan's two sisters and his hospital visit fuel speculation of a possible political understanding with Pakistan's military establishment

PTI ready to make peace?

Nawaz Sharif , Benazir Bhutto precedent

Why a deal may not be straightforward

Is Pakistan witnessing the first signs of a possible thaw between jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and the country's powerful military establishment? The release of two of his sisters and his recent hospital visit for eye treatment have come amid speculation that a political settlement involving Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has taken place.His sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were released on Thursday from Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail after the Punjab government withdrew their extended detention orders. The two had spent 53 days in custody after being detained ahead of a Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) protest march. Their sister Aleema Khan remains behind bars.The release came a day after Imran Khan was taken from Adiala Jail to Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for an eye examination and treatment. Doctors administered an injection for an issue affecting his right eye, besides treating his blood pressure. He was discharged in the early hours of Thursday and returned to prison.The developments have coincided with renewed speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, however, dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday, saying Khan and his family would receive whatever relief the courts granted them.The possibility of a rapprochement is not entirely new. In August, one of Imran Khan's closest aides, PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari, had told Reuters that the former prime minister would not confront the military if released."If Imran Khan was released tomorrow, hypothetically, he wouldn't do anything that would effectively damage the country," Bukhari had said, describing him as "magnanimous".He had also suggested that Munir could take the initiative to ease tensions, saying the army chief could extend a "healing hand" to the country."That doesn't mean you go loggerheads with the establishment, with the military leader," Bukhari said, adding that personal grievances could be set aside in the national interest.The remarks marked a notable shift in the PTI's public rhetoric after years of confrontation with the military establishment following Khan's ouster in a no-confidence vote in 2022.Bukhari, however, had mentioned that there were no talks between the PTI and the military. He also acknowledged that it was unclear whether Khan himself shared the willingness to reconcile being expressed by party leaders outside prison.The latest speculation has also been fuelled by opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai's claim in October that Khan could be facing pressure to accept an arrangement similar to those involving former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto.Sharif left Pakistan in 2000 after being ousted and imprisoned following the military coup led by General Pervez Musharraf. Bhutto spent years abroad in self-imposed exile after her government was dismissed in 1996.Achakzai alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz and Pakistan Peoples Party were part of a political arrangement that could pave the way for a similar outcome in Khan's case. However, he did not establish that any such agreement had been reached.An exile arrangement could potentially offer a way out of the prolonged confrontation, but there is no confirmation that Khan has agreed to leave Pakistan or that negotiations with Munir are under way.Imran Khan's relationship with the military establishment deteriorated after disagreements over key appointments and foreign policy. He has accused the military leadership, including Munir, of orchestrating his removal. The military denies interfering in politics.Despite being in prison since August 2023, Khan remains the central figure in Pakistan's political confrontation. His party continues to demand his release, access to family members and lawyers, and relief in the cases against him.The PTI's position also raises a crucial question: can its leadership outside prison negotiate or signal a compromise without Khan's explicit approval? Bukhari's August remarks came with the caveat that the former prime minister's own thinking might be different.For now, the signals remain contradictory. Two members of Khan's family have been released, he has received medical treatment, and a senior PTI aide has previously spoken of reconciliation. But the government has denied any political bargain, and there is no evidence of direct negotiations with Munir.Whether the latest developments represent isolated legal and medical decisions or the beginning of a fresh political opening remains the question.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's two sisters were released from jail on Thursday after 53 days in custody. He was also taken to a hospital for an eye examination and treatment. The developments have fuelled speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday.

Article Title: 74 militants killed in Pakistan security operations along Afghan border in 10 days
Article Text:
43 militants killed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa raids, 31 in Balochistan operations: Pakistan

Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in a series of raids and operations in the country's northwest and southwest regions bordering Afghanistan over the past 10 days, the Associated Press cited military officials Friday.The raids were conducted in Mir Ali and Orakzai districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where troops killed 43 militants and recovered weapons, ammunition and explosive devices, the military said in a statement.Separately, security forces killed 31 militants in multiple operations in Balochistan province since November 3, the military said. The province has been witnessing a bloody insurgency led by the rebel Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).Kabul has denied accusations of providing support to militant groups operating against Pakistan.The Pakistani Taliban are a separate group from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban, who returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Several TTP leaders and fighters are believed to be operating from sanctuaries across the Afghan border, a longstanding source of tension between Islamabad and Kabul.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in a series of raids and operations in the country's northwest and southwest regions bordering Afghanistan. At least 11 people were killed and three others injured after a vehicle veered off a mountainous road and plunged into a river in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir's Gilgit-Baltistan region, news agency AP reported, citing rescue officials and police.The accident took place on Thursday night after the driver lost control of the vehicle, local police official Mohammad Afzal said.Rescue teams continued search and rescue operations into early Friday. Article Title: BLA claims 18 killed in suicide vehicle attack on Pakistan Army camp in Balochistan
Article Text:
Baloch Liberation Army claims responsibility for a suicide vehicle attack on a Pakistani Army camp in Balochistan, claiming 18 personnel were killed

NEW DELHI: Multiple casualties were reported in a VBIED attack at Pak army’s main camp in Mastung, Balochistan Thursday. The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) took responsibility for the attack, claiming to have eliminated 18 personnel.According to BLA, its Fidayeen attack, the Majeed Brigade, carried out an operation in the Kanak area of Mastung, targeting a Pakistani military camp with a suicide vehicle-borne improvised explosive device followed by an assault by its armed fighters who entered the premises and targeted military personnel.The attack unfolded while a meeting of senior Pak Army personnel including colonel rank officials was underway when the mini-truck laden with explosives rammed into the main gate of the camp.The area has been on the boil since Wednesday. According to pro-BLA accounts on Telegram, Pak security forces were carrying out “operation Radd-ul-Fitna”, aimed at destroying tunnels allegedly made by Baloch rebels, on Wednesday and Thursday in the area.They claimed to have destroyed seven tunnels and seized arms, ammunition and explosives. In Musakhel, unidentified set ablaze construction machinery and a separate explosion destroyed a bridge in Mastung.On Wednesday, 13 Pakistani police personnel including a Deputy Superintendent of Police were killed after fighters from the rebel group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a major attack targeting mobile police units in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
